source: T-6A Techniques and Procedures Manual (I.N. T-6A 02/14, Change 9 Jul 22)

sections.title: Introduction to This Manual
sections.technique_summary: This manual provides the basic techniques and procedures necessary to safely and effectively employ the T-6. It provides the basis for development of the necessary physical skills and mental aptitude required to fly the T-6. The skills developed in the T-6 are applicable to flying any military A/C and provide the foundation for all follow-on flying training. GR 1T-6A-11 contains detailed instructions for inspections, checks, and procedures, and detailed information on A/C systems and systems operation; the GR and this publication complement each other.
sections.notes: Reference/administrative section; no graded item mapping.

sections.title: How to Use This Manual
sections.technique_summary: The manual is organized in an order that parallels the training flow in pilot training. The first five chapters cover topics applicable to every sortie and the second six chapters cover topics by category of flight. During subsequent stages of training, study centers on specific category chapters. Regular review of previous material is required.

parameters.name: chapters applicable to every sortie
parameters.verbatim: The first five chapters cover topics applicable to every sortie and the second six chapters cover topics by category of flight.

corrections: Regular review of previous material is required.

sections.title: Concept
sections.technique_summary: The concepts in Chapter 1 apply to every kind of sortie flown in the T-6 and many are universally applicable to flight in every type of military A/C. The topics presented cover overarching principles related to flying in general and flight training in the T-6 specifically. Full understanding of these general concepts is developed through study and flying experience, therefore regular review of this chapter is required.
corrections: Regular review of this chapter is required.

sections.title: Safety
sections.technique_summary: Safety is a critical component of successful mission accomplishment on every sortie. The safety mindset of each crew member is a key part in the overall safety of any flying operation. Each individual is responsible for minimizing risk to the people and assets under their control and for identifying potential safety hazards.
procedure_steps: Minimize risk to the people and assets under your control.
Identify potential safety hazards.

sections.title: Ground Safety
sections.technique_summary: The flight line is an extremely busy environment. Moving A/C, support equipment and emergency vehicles create a hazardous environment. Extra diligence is required to prevent a tragic event.
procedure_steps: Stay clear of the A/C danger areas as depicted in GR 1T-6A-11, Section 2 (prop areas and/or the jet exhaust of running A/C).
Secure loose items prior to entering the flight line to prevent foreign object damage (FOD).
Maintain constant watch for moving vehicles.
common_errors: Entering A/C danger areas (prop areas and/or the jet exhaust of running A/C).
Loose items not secured prior to entering the flight line, leading to foreign object damage (FOD).
Failure to maintain constant watch for moving vehicles on the flight line.

sections.title: Flying Safety
sections.technique_summary: Once airborne, safety assumes a more dynamic character; a converging A/C may unexpectedly appear or a malfunction can cause distractions during a critical phase of flight. Safe operation requires an aggressive disposition towards gaining and maintaining situational awareness. Situational awareness is an aircrew member's continuous perception of self and A/C in relation to the dynamic environment of flight, threats, and mission, and the ability to forecast, then execute, tasks based upon that perception.
procedure_steps: Clear the airspace.
Monitor A/C systems.
Establish and maintain an emergency recovery plan before an emergency occurs.
common_errors: Allowing a malfunction or an unexpected converging A/C to cause distraction during a critical phase of flight.
Failure to establish an emergency recovery plan before an emergency occurs.

sections.title: Flight Discipline
sections.technique_summary: Flight discipline is at the core of every flying operation. Maintaining the highest standards of integrity, professional military pilots must adhere to the spirit and intent of governing guidelines while executing the mission in the presence of temptation to do otherwise. It spans mission preparation, briefing, execution from engine start to engine shutdown, and the debriefing.
procedure_steps: Mission preparation: know the rules and procedures, study the profile, ensure crew rest requirements are met, and show up prepared to fly.
Briefing: be on time, be ready to discuss the mission and/or be ready to brief; ensure all questions are answered and mission requirements are understood.
In the air: execute the mission as briefed in accordance with governing guidelines, from engine start to engine shutdown.
Debriefing: flight discipline should be evaluated and specifically addressed during every mission debriefing.
common_errors: Showing up unprepared to fly — one unprepared crew-member can jeopardize the mission.
Crew rest requirements not met.
Not being on time or not ready to discuss/brief the mission.
Leaving questions unanswered or mission requirements not understood.
Not executing the mission as briefed in accordance with governing guidelines.

sections.title: Checklist Discipline
sections.technique_summary: GR 1T-6A-11CL, The Pilot's Pocket Checklist, is a condensed version of GR 1T-6A-11. The omission of a checklist item could lead to a dangerous situation; therefore positively confirm completion of all checklists regardless of how they are accomplished (for example, memory aid, mnemonic, approved unit-developed checklist or flight crew checklist). One technique to ensure accomplishment of every step is to execute a few items from memory then reference the checklist page to verify completion. Another technique is to complete the entire checklist and then refer back to the checklist to verify completion.

parameters.name: checklist restart point after interruption
parameters.value: two to three steps prior to the missed or interrupted step
parameters.verbatim: good techniques to get back on track include restarting at the first step of the checklist or restarting two to three steps prior to the missed or interrupted checklist step.

procedure_steps: Positively confirm completion of all checklists, regardless of how they are accomplished.
It is not necessary to refer to the checklist during critical phases of flight.
There will be only one pilot actively controlling the A/C at any point in time; this pilot is the pilot flying (PF), who is responsible for completion of all checklists.

Checklist items marked '(BOTH)' must be completed in both the front and rear cockpit: the PF initiates a '(BOTH)' item by challenging the pilot not flying (PNF); the item is not complete until a proper response is received from the PNF (challenge and response).
Once started, attempt to complete checklists without interruption.
If interrupted or an item was omitted, restart at the first step of the checklist or restart two to three steps prior to the missed or interrupted step.
Do not start a new checklist until completing the previous one.
common_errors: Omission of a checklist item — could lead to a dangerous situation.
Failure to positively confirm completion of all checklists.
Treating a '(BOTH)' item as complete without receiving a proper response from the PNF.
Starting a new checklist before completing the previous one.
Giving lip service to performing a checklist when using a standardized phrase or mnemonic instead of actually performing the checklist item or required check.
corrections: Execute a few items from memory then reference the checklist page to verify completion; or complete the entire checklist and then refer back to it to verify completion.
If interrupted, restart at the first step of the checklist or two to three steps prior to the missed or interrupted step.

sections.title: Single-Engine Mentality
sections.technique_summary: The T-6 engine has an excellent record of reliability, but the potential for engine loss deserves special consideration. Two options are available during an engine failure: forced landing or eject. Emergency landing pattern (ELP) practice increases the chance of successful recovery; however, the A/C is fitted with a highly capable and proven ejection seat that should be used if there is any doubt about safe recovery.

parameters.name: minimum ejection altitude planning aid
parameters.verbatim: Set a minimum ejection altitude when immediate ejection isn't warranted. This altitude is based on energy level (altitude/airspeed), configuration, and position relative to a suitable emergency airfield. When on profile consider using O-R-M-3-2-1.

parameters.name: engine restart decision criteria
parameters.verbatim: Consider the time delay and altitude lost between restart initiation and usable torque, the risk of fire, the presence of FOD and whether or not the engine is seized. (Often referred to as fire, FOD, or frozen.)

procedure_steps: Exercise extra vigilance for and a more conservative response to unusual engine indications; with unusual engine indications, recover to a suitable airfield.
Maintain awareness of nearest suitable emergency airfields during all phases of flight.
Include field elevation in the calculation of available glide distance.
Consider intervening terrain along the route of flight to emergency airfields.

Do not shut down the engine in flight if it is producing useable torque unless it is confirmed on fire, vibrating excessively with indications of impending failure, or not required for recovery to the selected emergency airfield.
Set a minimum ejection altitude when immediate ejection isn't warranted, based on energy level (altitude/airspeed), configuration, and position relative to a suitable emergency airfield.
Determine if engine restarts should be attempted (fire, FOD, or frozen).
Consider winds and weather on the recovery route and at the emergency airfield.
Select update points to assess the progress of the ELP glide profile; eject if it becomes apparent that recovery to an emergency airfield is not possible.
common_errors: Shutting down the engine in flight while it is still producing useable torque (not confirmed on fire, not vibrating excessively with indications of impending failure, and still required for recovery).
Failing to include field elevation in the calculation of available glide distance.
Ignoring intervening terrain along the route of flight to emergency airfields.
Not maintaining awareness of nearest suitable emergency airfields during all phases of flight.
Not setting a minimum ejection altitude when immediate ejection isn't warranted.
Attempting recovery when it is apparent that recovery to an emergency airfield is not possible, instead of ejecting.
corrections: With unusual engine indications, recover to a suitable airfield.
Eject if it becomes apparent that recovery to an emergency airfield is not possible.
Use the ejection seat if there is any doubt about safe recovery.

sections.title: Cockpit/Crew Resource Management (CRM)
sections.technique_summary: The CRM program is designed to develop aircrew skills in recognizing and responding to the conditions that lead to aircrew error. While flying, CRM is the effective use of all available resources to safely and efficiently accomplish mission objectives. CRM focuses aircrew members on agencies, procedures, and resources available to enable mission success; locally developed CRM checklists describe behaviours to reinforce and others to avoid.

parameters.name: number of CRM skills
parameters.verbatim: CRM centers on the following six skills

procedure_steps: Situational Awareness. Continuous perception of self and A/C in relation to the dynamic environment of flight, threats, and mission, and the ability to forecast, then execute tasks based upon that perception.

Flight Integrity/Wingman Consideration. Utilization of all members of a flight to accomplish the mission; wingman consideration requires flight members to recognize each other's limitations and plan or act accordingly.

Task Management. Ability to establish priorities and alter a course of action based on new information; includes management of automation, effective use of available resources, checklist discipline, and compliance with standard operating procedures.
Communications. Sharing of information with others to cause action; communications may direct, inform, question, or persuade.

Risk Management or Decision Making. Logic-based, common sense approach to decision making based on human, material, and environmental factors; the goal is to match risk to the mission, not completely eliminate risk.
Mission Planning, Briefing and Debriefing. Includes mission analysis and planning, briefing, and post mission debrief.
Include a CRM topic in the mission brief, tailored to specific mission requirements or conditions, and evaluate it during the debrief.
common_errors: Failure to recognize and respond to the conditions that lead to aircrew error.
Not using all available resources to safely and efficiently accomplish mission objectives.
Failure to recognize each other's limitations and plan or act accordingly (wingman consideration).
Failure to establish priorities or alter a course of action based on new information.
Non-compliance with standard operating procedures and checklist discipline.
Attempting to completely eliminate risk rather than matching risk to the mission.
sections.notes: The manual's six CRM skills map directly onto the CRM row of every category gradesheet. The manual prints 'permission analysis and planning' at 1.8.1.f; read as 'mission analysis' (apparent typo).

sections.title: Operational Risk Management (ORM)
sections.technique_summary: Flying is inherently risky. ORM is the process used to identify and reduce the risks of flying to an acceptable level. ORM trades off training benefit versus risk. Risk can often be minimized by mission changes that do not negatively impact training.
procedure_steps: Assess environmental conditions (for example, weather, bird status, index of thermal stress).
Assess mission profile (for example, formation, VFR, low level, use of uncontrolled airfields).
Assess pilot factors (for example, experience level, fatigue, currency).
common_errors: Failure to identify and reduce the risks of flying to an acceptable level.
Not considering environmental conditions, mission profile, or pilot factors in the risk assessment.
corrections: Minimize risk by mission changes that do not negatively impact training.

sections.title: Mission Preparation
sections.technique_summary: Mission success is directly related to mission preparation. There are four areas of mission preparation: General Study, Mission Selection, Mission Specific Study, and Mission Planning.

parameters.name: areas of mission preparation
parameters.verbatim: There are four areas of mission preparation

procedure_steps: General Study.
Mission Selection.
Mission Specific Study.
Mission Planning.

sections.title: General Study
sections.technique_summary: Study in general areas builds a foundation of knowledge for pilot training, other formal training courses, and operational missions. Some topics such as the flight manual are aircraft specific and other topics such as local area procedures are location specific. Areas of study including instrument rules and procedures (Instrument Flight Procedures), weather, aerodynamics, FLIP, and navigation are generic because they apply to any A/C, at any location, flying any type of mission. General study is a continuous process that is an integral part of a successful career in military aviation.

sections.title: Mission Selection
sections.technique_summary: Preparation cannot be focused until there is a specific mission. In formal training courses missions are normally determined by a syllabus, but missions are often tailored to individual training needs by reviewing the student grade book or training folder. Mission selection consists of objective setting and then profile selection. Objectives focus training to specific areas that must be accomplished to make the mission successful; the profile is the exact list of manoeuvres performed on a particular sortie.

parameters.name: parts of a valid objective
parameters.verbatim: A valid objective is realistic, achievable, measurable, and it has three stated or implied parts

parameters.name: example objective conditions
parameters.verbatim: Conditions. Starting parameters; for example, begin the loop with MAX power and 250 KIAS.

procedure_steps: Set the overall mission objective — the big picture: what must occur for the sortie to be successful (usually pulled from the syllabus in a formal training course).
Set training objectives that are specific and help determine success in relation to the syllabus, course training standards, continuation training requirements, etc.
Performance. Describes action and is specific; for example: no-flap landing, loop, and formation takeoff.
Conditions. Starting parameters; for example, begin the loop with MAX power and 250 KIAS.

Standards. The required parameters to meet during the execution of a manoeuvre, based on the flight manual, this manual, course training standards, current directives, or the level of proficiency demonstrated previously by the pilot.
Select the profile — the exact list of manoeuvres performed on the sortie.
common_errors: Objectives that are not realistic, achievable, and measurable.
Objectives lacking stated or implied performance, conditions, and standards.
sections.notes: The Performance / Conditions / Standards structure matches the execution-conditions-criteria structure of the gradesheet items.

sections.title: Mission Specific Study
sections.technique_summary: Study in areas specifically related to the mission, including general study areas relevant to that mission (for example, study of Instrument Flight Procedures before an instrument training sortie). Specific study also includes chair flying — a mental review of the sortie, visualization of specific manoeuvres and techniques, and mental review of checklists and specific tasks. Review individual manoeuvres, in appropriate sections of the flight manual and this manual, before each sortie.
procedure_steps: Review operational restrictions for the type of sortie.
Review approach plates (IAP).
Review local area procedures for that sortie.
Review the manoeuvres to be flown.
Cover daily study topics (for example, emergency procedure (EP) of the day).
Chair fly the sortie: visualize specific manoeuvres and techniques and mentally review checklists and specific tasks.
Focus study on the primary mission, but devote some time to possible alternate missions.
common_errors: Failing to review individual manoeuvres in the flight manual and this manual before each sortie.
Devoting no time to possible alternate missions.

sections.title: Mission Planning
sections.technique_summary: Mission planning includes all the tasks that turn the plan into reality — the tasks that must be accomplished to execute the specific mission on a specific day.
procedure_steps: Check notices to Airman (NOTAMs), weather, and operations notes.
Sign off Go/No-Go (items that must be accomplished before flying): flight crew information file (FCIF); squadron or pilot read files (CRF).
Check local profile, call sign, etc.
Schedule or reserve airspace (limited special use airspace, low level route, etc.).
Check bird hazard models.
Call destination if flying to an airfield other than the home airfield.
Review local restrictions (ramp freeze, construction, etc.).
Prepare individual briefing (briefing board, EP of the day, etc.).
Compute takeoff and landing data (TOLD).
Compute or check weight and balance.
Plan fuel, select route and file a flight plan.
common_errors: Go/No-Go items (FCIF, read files) not signed off before flying.
TOLD not computed; weight and balance not computed or checked.
NOTAMs, weather, or operations notes not checked.
Local restrictions (ramp freeze, construction) or bird hazard models not reviewed.

sections.title: Fuel Considerations
sections.technique_summary: Unlike many operational and training A/C, the T-6 is not fuel limited on most training sorties. Generally, syllabus directives, not available fuel, determine the duration of most sorties; however, regular fuel checks are still required and are an important part of each mission. Bingo, joker, and normal recovery fuels are defined in Training Basic Order 3-1.

parameters.name: fuels briefed every mission
parameters.value: bingo fuel and at least one joker fuel
parameters.verbatim: Bingo fuel and at least one joker fuel is briefed on every mission. Joker fuel is set at pre-planned transition points in the sortie. A mission may require several joker fuels.

parameters.name: bingo/joker/recovery fuel definitions reference
parameters.verbatim: Bingo, joker, and normal recovery fuels are defined in Training Basic Order 3-1.

procedure_steps: Brief bingo fuel and at least one joker fuel on every mission; set joker fuel at pre-planned transition points in the sortie.
Perform regular fuel checks throughout the mission.
If bingo fuel is reached, initiate recovery to arrive at the intended destination with the required fuel.
On most T-6 syllabus training sorties, initiate recovery prior to reaching bingo fuel due to sortie duration limitations.
The A/C commander (AC) of a single ship mission or the flight lead (FL) of a formation may adjust joker and/or bingo fuels during flight to accommodate mission conditions.
common_errors: Omitting regular fuel checks.
Not briefing bingo fuel and at least one joker fuel.
Failing to initiate recovery when bingo fuel is reached.
corrections: If bingo fuel is reached, initiate recovery to arrive at the intended destination with the required fuel.
Adjust joker and/or bingo fuels in flight (AC or FL) when mission priorities and flight conditions change.

sections.title: Mission Briefing
sections.technique_summary: The AC or FL may or may not be the actual briefer, but in every case will ensure that each mission is thoroughly briefed and debriefed. Briefings set the tone for all missions. The briefing should focus on how to successfully accomplish the established objectives.
procedure_steps: All crewmembers will be on time, prepared, and in possession of all required material and information.
Complete all preflight administrative tasks (such as checking the weather and the NOTAMs) before the briefing.
As a minimum, cover all required items using locally established briefing guides.
Discuss formal special interest items (SII) during all briefings.
Other crewmembers or formation members will be prepared to assist the AC or FL.
Focus the briefing on how to successfully accomplish the established objectives.
common_errors: Arriving late, unprepared, or without all required material and information.
Preflight administrative tasks (weather, NOTAMs) not completed before the briefing.
Formal special interest items (SII) not discussed.
Briefing that does not focus on how to successfully accomplish the established objectives.

sections.title: Debriefing
sections.technique_summary: The purpose of debriefing is to determine if mission objectives were achieved. From both administrative and tactical perspectives, the AC and/or FL should analyse root causes of errors and how they will be corrected, address all questions and concerns, and emphasize major learning points.
procedure_steps: Analyse root causes of errors, and how they will be corrected.
Address all questions, concerns.
Emphasize major learning points.
common_errors: Debriefing errors without analysing their root causes or how they will be corrected.
Leaving questions and concerns unaddressed.

sections.title: Tandem Seat Challenges
sections.technique_summary: Limited visibility of the crewmember in the other cockpit makes it difficult to judge intentions, anticipate actions, and verify A/C systems configuration. Verbal communication must compensate for the lack of inter-cockpit visibility. Most functions are controllable from either cockpit; however some items can only be manipulated or directly checked in the front cockpit.

parameters.name: FCP-only systems
parameters.value: auxiliary battery activation; manual fuel balance L/R switch; ECS controls; parking brake position; emergency gear extension; firewall shutoff handle
parameters.verbatim: Activation of the auxiliary battery- FCP; Manual fuel balance L/R switch - FCP; Environmental control system (ECS) controls - FCP; Parking brake position - FCP; Emergency gear extension - FCP; Firewall Shutoff Handle - FCP

parameters.name: RCP-only system
parameters.verbatim: Interseat sequencing system (ISS) - RCP

parameters.name: independently set in each cockpit
parameters.verbatim: Altimeter settings are independently set in each cockpit - FCP and RCP

procedure_steps: Know which systems are controlled from the FCP or RCP and can only be monitored or controlled from the opposite cockpit through verbal or visual coordination.
Check bleed air inflow by pressing the G-suit test button.
Confirm OBOGS operations are on by turning off the supply lever.
Confirm defog operation by sound or temperature of the piccolo tubes.
Confirm external light operation (on the ground) by looking for reflections from adjacent A/C or other surfaces.
Consider FCP pilot landing if RCP visibility is severely compromised.
Ensure all crewmembers thoroughly understand transfer of A/C and/or systems control.
common_errors: Failing to compensate with verbal communication for the lack of inter-cockpit visibility — misjudging intentions, failing to anticipate actions, and failing to verify A/C systems configuration.
Not knowing which systems are controlled only from the FCP or only from the RCP.
Altimeter settings not coordinated (they are set independently in each cockpit).
corrections: Consider FCP pilot landing if RCP visibility is severely compromised.

sections.title: Transfer of A/C and Systems Control
sections.technique_summary: Only one pilot, at a time, can fly the A/C. It is vital for flight safety to clearly establish who is the PF and who is the PNF, as fatal accidents have occurred when two pilots attempted to fly the A/C simultaneously. The PF is responsible for checklist completion and systems operation; however, the PF may task the PNF to operate systems. Using the exact words is critical to establish proper habit patterns that enhance swift, unambiguous transfer of A/C control.

parameters.name: transfer phraseology
parameters.value: "You have the A/C" / "I have the A/C"
parameters.verbatim: The PF relinquishing control says, "You have the A/C." The PNF assumes control and says, "I have the A/C," and noticeably shakes the control stick.

procedure_steps: The PF relinquishing control says, 'You have the A/C.'
The PNF assumes control, says 'I have the A/C,' and noticeably shakes the control stick.

The order may be reversed as the AC always retains the authority to take A/C control when required; if the AC as PNF says 'I have the A/C' and noticeably shakes the control stick, the PF must immediately relinquish control and say 'You have the A/C.'
The order of transfer is less important than each crewmember executing his/her role in accordance with the procedures listed.

In the event of intercom failure, the PF signals the desire to relinquish A/C control by smoothly pushing the rudder pedals in a back and forth motion, and the PNF assumes control by vigorously shaking the control stick. As a technique, the pilot relinquishing control raises both hands in the air for the other pilot to see, either directly from the RCP or using mirrors from the FCP.
Never relinquish control of the A/C until the other pilot has positively assumed control (shaken the control stick).
Do not hesitate to relinquish control when directed by the IP.
Immediately query the other crewmember in case of confusion.

Coordinate systems use to avoid inadvertent inputs on canopy, radio management unit (RMU), global positioning system (GPS) and electronic flight instrument system (EFIS) configuration; the PF controls all systems unless a transfer of that system has been clearly communicated, and the PNF should communicate when transferring the system back to the PF.
common_errors: Two pilots attempting to fly the A/C simultaneously — fatal accidents have occurred.
Use of other words such as 'it' or 'jet' in lieu of the term 'A/C' — they can be misunderstood, misheard, and create confusion.
Relinquishing control before the other pilot has positively assumed control (shaken the control stick).
Hesitating to relinquish control when directed by the IP.
Inadvertent inputs caused by the 'last use, last in control' setup of T-6 systems when systems use is not coordinated (canopy, RMU, GPS, EFIS).
corrections: Immediately query the other crewmember in case of confusion.
Use the exact words to establish proper habit patterns for swift, unambiguous transfer of A/C control.

sections.title: Clearing
sections.technique_summary: Each crewmember is responsible for collision avoidance regardless of rank, experience, or cockpit position, whether IFR or VFR. The two primary tools for clearing in the T-6 are eyes and radios. ATC shares A/C separation responsibility with the pilot and provides separation between IFR and participating VFR A/C operating in controlled airspace; the use of radar monitoring, assigned flying areas, or ATC separation can assist in but does not relieve pilots of the responsibility to clear. Visual detection is the most important factor in clearing for other A/C.

parameters.name: visual scan arc
parameters.verbatim: Visual Scanning. Search an area with an arc of approximately 20-30° at a time and focus on a distant point (cloud, ground reference, etc.) within the arc for 3-5 seconds.

parameters.name: focus dwell time per arc
parameters.verbatim: focus on a distant point (cloud, ground reference, etc.) within the arc for 3-5 seconds

parameters.name: natural eye focus distance after instrument crosscheck
parameters.verbatim: After crosschecking instruments in the cockpit, it is necessary to refocus on a distant point because the eye will naturally focus at a distance of about 18 inches.

parameters.name: minimum flight path clearance from other A/C
parameters.verbatim: Ensure the intended flight path is well clear of other A/C (500 feet minimum).

parameters.name: clearing turn magnitude
parameters.value: high bank angles or turns of approximately 90° off the established heading
parameters.verbatim: Clearing turns can consist of turns that include high bank angles or turns of approximately 90° off the established heading.

procedure_steps: Visual Scanning. Search an area with an arc of approximately 20-30° at a time and focus on a distant point within the arc for 3-5 seconds; after crosschecking instruments, refocus on a distant point.

Heading Changes. On a collision course another A/C appears stationary in the canopy and is difficult to see; slight heading changes create the relative movement required for detection. Most effective when ATC provides traffic alerts for A/C not acquired visually.
Wing Flashes. When an A/C is known to be close but not visually acquired, a wing flash or rock can create the necessary movement for detection.

Radio. Use position reports or position information to narrow visual clearing efforts to specific quadrants. Knowledge of local area traffic can also cue crewmembers to the most likely areas of potential conflict.
If the PNF sees a hazard, point it out immediately to the PF (for example, 'traffic, right 2 o'clock low, tracking right to left').
If time is critical and collision is imminent, the PNF should take control of the A/C and avoid the hazard, ensuring the intended flight path is well clear of other A/C (500 feet minimum).
Be aware of the restrictions to visibility created by the canopy bows.
Use clearing turns when warranted to clear blind spots beneath the A/C fuselage and wings, especially in training areas.
In the traffic pattern, know the choke points and comply with mandatory radio transmissions ('clearing on the radios').
common_errors: Relying on radar monitoring, assigned flying areas, or ATC separation — these assist in but do not relieve the pilot of the responsibility to clear.
Failing to refocus on a distant point after crosschecking instruments (the eye naturally focuses at about 18 inches).
Failing to detect an A/C on a collision course because it appears stationary in the canopy.
Channelizing on radio position information instead of prioritizing — the accuracy of the information provided can vary depending on specific conditions and capabilities.
Not accounting for the restrictions to visibility created by the canopy bows.
Not clearing blind spots beneath the A/C fuselage and wings, especially in training areas.
Non-compliance with mandatory radio transmissions in the pattern — they serve as position reports essential to pattern deconfliction.
PNF failing to point out a hazard immediately to the PF.
corrections: Use slight heading changes to create the relative movement required to detect an A/C on a collision course.
Use a wing flash or rock when an A/C is known to be close but not visually acquired.
Use clearing turns (high bank angles or approximately 90° off the established heading) to clear blind spots.
If collision is imminent, the PNF takes control and avoids the hazard, staying well clear (500 feet minimum).
sections.notes: Choke points listed: Military A/C — VFR entry, Initial Point to South-North Point, downwind, high-to-Low Key and the perch point; Civilian A/C — pattern entry, downwind, and final. Local traffic patterns present the greatest collision potential. Figures 1.1-1.3 give clock positions and FCP canopy code (elevation and azimuth).

sections.title: G-Awareness
sections.technique_summary: The T-6 is flown in a variety of flight regimes that result in rapidly changing G-forces. To avoid grey out, blackout, or G-induced loss of consciousness (GLOC) an effective anti-G straining manoeuvre is essential. Physical fitness, adequate rest, and proper hydration can improve G-tolerance.
common_errors: Ineffective anti-G straining manoeuvre, leading to grey out, blackout, or G-induced loss of consciousness (GLOC).
corrections: Improve G-tolerance through physical fitness, adequate rest, and proper hydration.

sections.title: Anti-G Straining Manoeuvre (AGSM)
sections.technique_summary: Accomplish the AGSM by firmly contracting muscles of the legs, abdomen, and chest. As the amount of G increases, increase the intensity of the strain, and attempt to exhale through a closed airway. Continue to strain and simultaneously breathe approximately every 2 to 3 seconds. Think of the AGSM as a continuum: as the amount of G increases, increase the intensity of the strain and pay careful attention to proper breathing technique.

parameters.name: breathing interval during AGSM
parameters.verbatim: Continue to strain and simultaneously breathe approximately every 2 to 3 seconds.

parameters.name: maximum strain hold without breathing
parameters.verbatim: Do not hold the strain too long (more than 3 seconds) without breathing as this reduces G tolerance.

procedure_steps: Firmly contract muscles of the legs, abdomen, and chest.
As the amount of G increases, increase the intensity of the strain and attempt to exhale through a closed airway.
Continue to strain and simultaneously breathe approximately every 2 to 3 seconds.
If gray out occurs at the onset of G forces and altitude and/or airspeed are not critical, return to 1 G flight, reapply the anti-G strain, then continue manoeuvring.
common_errors: Holding the strain too long (more than 3 seconds) without breathing — this reduces G tolerance.
Not increasing the intensity of the strain as the amount of G increases.
Exceeding A/C or personal G-limits.
Applying the AGSM after gray out has already occurred at the onset of G forces — application may then not eliminate the gray out.
corrections: If gray out occurs at the onset of G forces and altitude and/or airspeed are not critical, return to 1 G flight, reapply the anti-G strain, and then continue manoeuvring.
Use caution not to exceed A/C or personal G-limits.

sections.title: AGSM Effectiveness
sections.technique_summary: It is important to start the AGSM before the onset of G-forces and maintain the strain throughout the period of increased G-loading. The amount of strain required varies with the amount of applied G-force. An effective AGSM uses full muscle contraction and keeps constant breathing cycles. Lower-G situations still require all elements of a full AGSM, but at a lower level of strain intensity.
procedure_steps: Start the AGSM before the onset of G-forces.
Maintain the strain throughout the period of increased G-loading.
Use full muscle contraction and keep constant breathing cycles.
In lower-G situations use all elements of a full AGSM, but at a lower level of strain intensity.
common_errors: Starting the AGSM after the onset of G-forces instead of before.
Not maintaining the strain throughout the period of increased G-loading.
Omitting elements of the full AGSM in lower-G situations.

sections.title: AGSM Demonstration
sections.technique_summary: The AGSM demonstration allows practice of the anti-G strain technique and familiarization with increased G-loading in a controlled setting. The demonstration consists of a series of turns, each at a constant G-level, with a break between turns for critique and rest. The manoeuvre is flown at gradually increasing G-levels, starting at 2 Gs and increasing to 4 Gs, depending on proficiency.

parameters.name: G-level progression
parameters.value: starting at 2 Gs and increasing to 4 Gs, depending on proficiency
parameters.verbatim: The manoeuvre is flown at gradually increasing G-levels, starting at 2 Gs and increasing to 4 Gs, depending on proficiency.

parameters.name: AGSM cycle duration
parameters.verbatim: The AGSM cycle should last from 10 to 15 seconds with at least 4 to 5 breathing cycles.

parameters.name: breathing cycles per AGSM cycle
parameters.verbatim: The AGSM cycle should last from 10 to 15 seconds with at least 4 to 5 breathing cycles.

procedure_steps: Fly a series of turns, each at a constant G-level, with a break between turns for critique and rest.
Fly at gradually increasing G-levels, starting at 2 Gs and increasing to 4 Gs, depending on proficiency.
Make the demonstration of sufficient duration to ensure a proper AGSM: 10 to 15 seconds per AGSM cycle with at least 4 to 5 breathing cycles.
If personal G-tolerance limits are approached at any time, inform the other crew-member.
common_errors: Demonstration of insufficient duration to ensure a proper AGSM.
Not informing the other crew-member when personal G-tolerance limits are approached.

sections.title: G-Awareness Exercise
sections.technique_summary: Accomplish a G-awareness exercise on sorties that include manoeuvres that require or may result in 3 or more Gs. It should be a level or slightly descending turn, using maximum power, begun with sufficient airspeed to sustain 4 Gs. The G-onset rate should be slow and smooth, allowing sufficient time to evaluate the effectiveness of the AGSM and determine G-tolerance.

parameters.name: trigger for G-awareness exercise
parameters.value: manoeuvres that require or may result in 3 or more Gs
parameters.verbatim: Accomplish a G-awareness exercise on sorties that include manoeuvres that require or may result in 3 or more Gs.

parameters.name: entry airspeed (planning)
parameters.verbatim: (For planning purposes, use approximately 200-220 KIAS minimum for a level to slightly descending turn where the nose remains within 10° of the horizon.)

parameters.name: nose position
parameters.verbatim: a level to slightly descending turn where the nose remains within 10° of the horizon

parameters.name: power
parameters.verbatim: The G-awareness exercise should be a level or slightly descending turn, using maximum power.

parameters.name: target G and duration
parameters.value: approximately 4 Gs maintained for approximately 4 to 5 breathing cycles
parameters.verbatim: Increase Gs to approximately 4 Gs and maintain for approximately 4 to 5 breathing cycles in order to allow full cardiovascular response.

parameters.name: G-load for advanced aerobatic and formation training
parameters.verbatim: For advanced aerobatic and formation training, the G-awareness exercise should be flown to G-loads of 4 to 5 Gs.

procedure_steps: Enter a level or slightly descending turn using maximum power, with sufficient airspeed to sustain 4 Gs (approximately 200-220 KIAS minimum, nose within 10° of the horizon).
Apply a slow and smooth G-onset rate, allowing sufficient time to evaluate AGSM effectiveness and determine G-tolerance.
Increase Gs to approximately 4 Gs and maintain for approximately 4 to 5 breathing cycles to allow full cardiovascular response.
For advanced aerobatic and formation training, fly the exercise to G-loads of 4 to 5 Gs.
common_errors: G-onset rate too rapid — it should be slow and smooth to allow sufficient time to evaluate the effectiveness of the AGSM and determine G-tolerance.
Insufficient entry airspeed to sustain 4 Gs.
Nose allowed outside 10° of the horizon during the exercise.
Not maintaining approximately 4 Gs for approximately 4 to 5 breathing cycles, so full cardiovascular response is not allowed.
Omitting the G-awareness exercise before manoeuvres that require or may result in 3 or more Gs.
corrections: If gray out begins during the demonstration, return to 1 G flight, re-evaluate the strain, and then smoothly re-enter the G-awareness exercise.
If personal G-tolerance is lower than required for the sortie, terminate high-G manoeuvring.
sections.notes: Referenced again in Chapter 6 (6.3) and Chapter 9 (9.11) as a prerequisite before any manoeuvre that may require three or more Gs.

sections.title: Radio Procedures
sections.technique_summary: The PF is responsible for all radio calls. The PNF may transmit without transfer of A/C control; however, the PF must be notified. EXCEPTION: instructors may immediately correct improper radio calls without first notifying the student. Pilots should attempt to use standard phraseology as much as practical; standard terminology minimizes radio congestion and facilitates effective communication.

parameters.name: radio call format
parameters.value: agency calling, call sign, location, and request
parameters.verbatim: Whenever possible, format radio calls as follows: agency calling, call sign, location, and request. For example, "KALAMATA APPROACH, PELOPS 17, PYLOS AREA 8-18, REQUEST RTB."

parameters.name: governing publications
parameters.value: DOC 9432 (Manual of Radiotelephony, ICAO), DOC 4444 (Air Traffic Management, ICAO), STANAG 3817, Communicational Manual and individual wing and/or squadron instructions
parameters.verbatim: Radio procedures, definitions, and guidance are contained in the following publications: DOC 9432 (Manual of Radiotelephony, ICAO), DOC 4444 (Air Traffic Management, ICAO), STANAG 3817, Communicational Manual and individual wing and/or squadron instructions.

procedure_steps: Clarity: voice what is required correctly through standard phraseology; comprehension is the single most important factor in pilot-controller communications. When uncertain of the meaning of standard phrases used by controlling agencies, clarify with plain language.
Brevity: provide controllers with the information needed, nothing more, nothing less, in the format expected.
Do not depress the microphone button during other transmissions; anticipate other party's replies to ATC and/or pilot transmissions and do not interrupt.
Avoid transmitting when another A/C is in a critical phase of flight (for example, in the flare).
Format radio calls as: agency calling, call sign, location, and request.
For a detailed request, first get the controller's attention (for example, 'KALAMATA APPROACH, PELOPS 17'), then state the request after the controller acknowledges.
The PNF may transmit without transfer of A/C control, but the PF must be notified.
common_errors: Use of non-standard and improvised phrasing — it contributes to miscommunication, misunderstood clearances and A/C mishaps, and should be minimized.

Adding verbiage that is not required, which clutters the radio frequency — meaningless phrases such as 'with you', 'checking in', 'with a flash', 'at this time', 'be advised', particularly on congested frequencies.
Omitting needed information, requiring the controller to query for the missing information — this also wastes airtime.
Depressing the microphone button during other transmissions / interrupting.
Transmitting when another A/C is in a critical phase of flight (for example, in the flare).
Making a long detailed request without first getting the controller's attention — causes confusion and frequency congestion.
PNF transmitting without notifying the PF.
corrections: When uncertain of the meaning of standard phrases used by controlling agencies, clarify with plain language.
Get the controller's attention first, then state the request after acknowledgement.
sections.notes: Instructors may immediately correct improper radio calls without first notifying the student.

sections.title: GPS Usage
sections.technique_summary: VOR and DME navigation skills will continue to be emphasized throughout all phases of training. To enhance follow-on training, GPS usage is introduced early in training. GPS should not be used as a primary source of navigation but as an advisory one.
procedure_steps: Use GPS as an advisory source of navigation only.
Continue to emphasize VOR and DME navigation skills throughout all phases of training.
common_errors: Using GPS as a primary source of navigation instead of as an advisory one.

sections.title: Emergency Procedures
sections.technique_summary: Three basic rules apply to all emergency procedures: 1) Remain calm and maintain A/C control, 2) Analyze the situation and take proper action, and 3) Land as soon as conditions permit. If the A/C cannot be recovered safely, ejection may be the only option. A successful conclusion to any emergency results from in-depth systems knowledge, sound judgment, and effective CRM.

parameters.name: prioritization memory aid
parameters.verbatim: One technique to help prioritize pilot action, that is applicable in normal and emergency situations, is the memory aid, "Aviate - Navigate - Communicate." Fly the A/C first!

procedure_steps: Remain calm and maintain A/C control. Fly the A/C; the PF flies the A/C until the AC directs otherwise. Maintain an A/C attitude that allows for an appropriate response to the emergency; set power and trim to help maintain control. A/C control may include the initial turn and/or climb to a recovery airfield.

Analyze the situation and take proper action. Confirm indications with the other crewmember. If the master warning/master caution light is illuminated, look at the CWS panel before resetting the MASTER WARNING / CAUTION LIGHT by pushing it to turn it off. Consider all indications when diagnosing the problem.
Critical Actions: boldface procedures shall be committed to memory and should be accomplished only after the pilot has positively identified the problem.
Noncritical Actions: checklist steps that contribute to an orderly sequence of events; warnings, cautions, and notes in the checklist must also be reviewed during checklist execution.
Communicate with ATC and the Supervisor of Flying (SOF).
Evaluate possible recovery airfields — the initial airfield selected may not always be the best.
Request a chase ship if useful.
Review approach/landing and post-landing actions with the other crewmember or ground-based agencies.
Land as soon as conditions permit.
common_errors: Resetting the MASTER WARNING / CAUTION LIGHT before looking at the CWS panel.
Not confirming indications with the other crewmember.
Performing boldface before the pilot has positively identified the problem.
Failing to consider all indications when diagnosing the problem.
Not reviewing warnings, cautions, and notes in the checklist during checklist execution.
Staying with the initially selected recovery airfield when changes to energy state or additional research identify a better option.
Landing on an unprepared surface or ditching — not recommended.
corrections: Fly the A/C first: 'Aviate - Navigate - Communicate.'
Set power and trim to help maintain control.
In many cases the proper actions are clear; however, alternate courses of action may exist depending on the nature of the emergency, flight conditions, and pilot proficiency.
Use ATC to identify suitable recovery airfields, find required frequencies, alert emergency response assets, identify hazardous weather, or help find a chase ship.
Use the SOF to read checklists, reference the flight manual, check calculations, identify potential chase ships, or offer advice on course of action and recovery plans.

Use a chase ship to lead A/C with instrument malfunctions through weather, provide ground-expert-like assistance, clear for a task saturated emergency A/C, handle communications with ATC, or inspect A/C areas which cannot be seen from either cockpit.
The PNF shall consult the checklist, monitor systems, provide advice, and maintain situational awareness on the nearest suitable landing field.
The flight crew checklist, in-flight guide, flight information handbook, or other flight information publications (FLIP) can contain useful information.
sections.notes: Flight manual landing definitions: Land As Soon As Possible — declare an emergency and land at the nearest suitable landing area considering severity of the emergency, weather conditions, field facilities, ambient lighting, and command guidance. Land As Soon As Practical — emergency conditions are less urgent; the mission is to be terminated but an immediate landing may not be necessary. Suitable Landing Area — a hard surface runway, taxiway, or under/overrun; landing on an unprepared surface or ditching is not recommended. The A/C commander determines who flies the A/C based on pilot workload and the experience level and ability of both pilots.

sections.title: Tabletop and Stand-up Emergency Procedures (EPs)
sections.technique_summary: The purpose of tabletop EPs is to expose student pilots to as many different emergency situations as possible on the ground, before they are faced with actually handling one while airborne. Stand-up EPs provide the same exposure but with the added pressure of performing while people are watching over your decisions, simulating the stress of an actual airborne emergency. The objective is to exercise your knowledge and available resources to formulate and execute a plan to get you safely on the ground. The mnemonic A-A-B-C-D-E-F helps put the basic EP principles into logical steps.

parameters.name: EP method mnemonic
parameters.verbatim: the use of the mnemonic A-A-B-C-D-E-F (Figure 1.4.) will help put the basic EP principles into logical steps.

parameters.name: FEVER check — fluctuating fuel flow threshold
parameters.verbatim: F stands for fluctuating fuel flow. A properly working engine at a constant PCL setting should not have fuel flow jumping around more than 10 pounds per hour (pph).

parameters.name: PEL first four steps
parameters.verbatim: perform the first four steps of the precautionary emergency landing (PEL) checklist (turn, climb, clean, check [TCCC]).

parameters.name: engine failure during flight boldface trim speed
parameters.verbatim: the engine failure during flight boldface will require you to trim the A/C to 125 KIAS

parameters.name: PCL threshold example in cleanup step
parameters.verbatim: if you perform the non-boldface oil system malfunction checklist when the PCL was at MAX, moving the PCL below 60 % will require the control stick, rudder, and PCL to be moved to compensate for less thrust.

parameters.name: ATC emergency report content
parameters.value: NTSB — nature of the emergency, time to landing, souls on board, and briefing (your plan of action)
parameters.verbatim: When you talk to ATC make sure you can tell them (easily memorized by the NTSB acronym): nature of the emergency, time to landing, souls on board, and briefing (your plan of action).

procedure_steps: A — A/C Control. Continue to fly the A/C and get to a stable flight condition that allows time to analyze the situation. In the Contact Phase this may involve a contact recovery or Out of Control Flight (OCF) recovery; in Low-Level Navigation it may involve starting a climb to the top of the route; in formation it may involve calling knock it off (KIO) and taking the number 1 position. Describe how you will use the control stick, rudder, and PCL to achieve a stabilized flight condition.

A — Analyze the Situation. Time stands still (TSS): ask the IP questions about the status of different A/C systems. Use acronyms such as the FEVER check for engine problems (Fluctuating fuel flow; Excessive interstage-turbine temperature (ITT); Visual indications — smoke, flames, oil on the windscreen; Erratic engine operation; Roughness). For an impending engine problem, perform the first four steps of the PEL checklist (turn, climb, clean, check [TCCC]), get the A/C on an ELP profile once pointed toward the nearest suitable airfield, and continue to analyze. Also analyze avionics, lights and tones, circuit breakers, and outside A/C structure (possibly via a chase ship).

B — Boldface. Once analyzed, time resumes: initially state the boldface steps then verbally execute them. Applying a boldface procedure should require you to do something with the A/C. Once complete, ensure the A/C is still under control and analyze the action — did the boldface do what it was intended to do (perform another FEVER check)? Then ask whether another boldface applies and continue in this loop until no more apply.

C — Cleanup items and/or Checklists. Perform the non-boldface (cleanup) steps of the boldface checklists and any other applicable non-boldface checklists. After each checklist, refer back to A/C control. Continue looping until no more checklists are required, then use the in-flight guide to determine any other pertinent data required to recover the A/C (for example, local NORDO procedures).

D — Declare, With a Plan. Once the game plan is established, let the appropriate authorities know what is wrong and what you plan to do. Tell ATC the nature of the emergency, time to landing, souls on board, and briefing (plan of action). Know the pattern type (straight-in, ELP, overhead, instrument approach) and how you are going to stop the A/C (stop on the runway and emergency ground egress, stop on a taxiway, or taxi back to parking).
E — Egress/Ejection. Review Emergency Ground Egress and Controlled Ejection Checklists. Determine when you will eject if the situation deteriorates and leads to an ejection scenario.
F — Follow the Plan. Continue to chair fly the emergency to a safe landing; talk the IP through all the steps, descent check, arrival and pattern procedures, and safely exit the A/C.
common_errors: Spending more time than necessary on the analysis just to stall for time — even though time stands still in the flight room, it does not in the A/C.
Performing boldface before analyzing the situation.
Not re-checking A/C control after applying a boldface or a checklist (for example, moving the PCL below 60 % requires control stick, rudder, and PCL compensation for less thrust).
Not verifying whether the boldface did what it was intended to do (failing to perform another FEVER check).
Failing to ask whether another boldface applies (for example, engine failure during flight may lead to immediate engine start).
Declaring without a plan, or being unable to state nature of the emergency, time to landing, souls on board, and plan of action to ATC.
Not determining in advance when you will eject if the situation deteriorates.
corrections: If you think you know what is wrong with the A/C, go with it — do not stall for time.
After each boldface or checklist, refer back to A/C control and re-analyze.
Use the in-flight guide to determine any other pertinent data required to recover the A/C.
sections.notes: Figure 1.4 A-A-B-C-D-E-F Method of Accomplishing Practice EPs. The text at 1.21.b refers to 'paragraph 1.19.' for the basic EP principles, but the Emergency Procedures section is numbered 1.20 in this edition — apparent internal cross-reference error in the manual.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.technique_summary: This chapter discusses basic terms that apply to all A/C. It explains concepts and terms associated with the T-6 as a single-engine, propeller-driven A/C. Knowledge and understanding of these terms and their associated aerodynamic effects is essential to successfully fly the T-6.
sections.notes: Chapter opener; no gradable content of its own.

sections.title: CONTROL EFFECTS
sections.technique_summary: Each flight control affects the attitude of the A/C by controlling movement about one of three axes. Control movements result in the same predictable A/C responses, regardless of the attitude of the A/C. The pilot is the approximate pivot point about which all changes of attitude occur.

parameters.name: vertical axis
parameters.verbatim: Vertical Axis Yaw

parameters.name: longitudinal axis
parameters.verbatim: Longitudinal Axis Roll

parameters.name: lateral axis
parameters.verbatim: Lateral Axis Pitch

sections.notes: Figure 2.1 Control Axes.

sections.title: USE OF CONTROLS
sections.technique_summary: When a control surface is moved out of its streamlined position, air flowing past it exerts pressure against the control surface and tries to return it to neutral. These air forces on control surfaces are felt on the control stick and rudder pedals. Control forces are directly proportional to airspeed and control deflection and provide feedback to the pilot. This feedback identifies trim requirements.

parameters.name: control force relationship
parameters.value: directly proportional to airspeed and control deflection
parameters.verbatim: Control forces are directly proportional to airspeed and control deflection and provide feedback to the pilot.

sections.notes: Air forces can impede positioning of the controls to the desired position.

sections.title: HOW TO USE THE RUDDER
sections.technique_summary: When properly positioned, the heels of the feet rest upon the cockpit floor and the balls of the feet touch the rudder pedals. Rudder application should be smooth, similar to application of brakes in an automobile. In order to optimize control feel, maintain firm but relaxed pressure on the rudders.
procedure_steps: Rest the heels of the feet upon the cockpit floor with the balls of the feet touching the rudder pedals.
Apply rudder smoothly, similar to application of brakes in an automobile.
Maintain firm but relaxed pressure on the rudders to optimize control feel.

sections.title: HOW TO USE THE CONTROL STICK
sections.technique_summary: Although many maneuvers generate heavy control stick forces, a firm but light touch on the control stick optimizes control feel. Hands and arms should remain relaxed. Ideally, during cruise operations fingertips on the control stick is all that should be needed. Fingertips give the best feedback on minute changes of A/C trim.
procedure_steps: Use a firm but light touch on the control stick; keep hands and arms relaxed.
During cruise operations use fingertips only on the control stick.

sections.title: HOW TO USE THE PCL (incl. Table 2.1 General Power Settings)
sections.technique_summary: Known power settings provide a useful starting point for PCL position. Starting with power settings close to the desired setting minimizes torque and propeller effects. General power settings are listed in Table 2.1; these pitch and power settings are approximate, and vary from A/C to A/C based on factors such as A/C weight, pressure altitude, and temperature. The PCL requires relatively little travel to change the power, so a small movement can result in a larger than desired power change.

parameters.name: level flight - 250 KIAS
parameters.value: 250 KIAS, gear UP, flaps UP, pitch 2 deg NL, power 93%

parameters.name: level flight - 200 KIAS
parameters.value: 200 KIAS, gear UP, flaps UP, pitch 0 deg, power 50% + altitude (see note)
parameters.verbatim: 200 0° 50% + altitude (see note)

parameters.name: level flight - 150 KIAS
parameters.value: 150 KIAS, gear UP, flaps UP, pitch 2 deg NH, power 32%
parameters.verbatim: Level Flight 150 UP UP 2°NH 32%

parameters.name: torque altitude correction (level flight 200 KIAS)
parameters.value: add MSL altitude in thousands to the torque setting
parameters.verbatim: NOTE: Add mean sea level (MSL) altitude (e.g., at 3,000 feet MSL, set 53% torque).

parameters.name: takeoff
parameters.value: 85 KIAS, gear DOWN, flaps TO, pitch 7-10 deg NH
parameters.verbatim: Takeoff 85 DOWN TO 7-10°NH

parameters.name: climb - 180 KIAS
parameters.value: 180 KIAS, gear UP, flaps UP, pitch 8 deg NH, power MAX, other ±1% per 1,000 feet

parameters.name: climb - 160 KIAS
parameters.value: 160 KIAS, gear UP, flaps UP, pitch 10 deg NH, power MAX, other ±1% per 1,000 feet

parameters.name: climb - 140 KIAS
parameters.value: 140 KIAS, gear UP, flaps UP, pitch 12 deg NH, power MAX, other ±1% per 1,000 feet
parameters.verbatim: Climb 140 UP UP 12°NH MAX ±1% per 1,000 feet

parameters.name: Table 2.1 legend
parameters.value: NH = nose high, NL = nose low, TO = takeoff flaps, MAX = maximum
parameters.verbatim: LEGEND: NH—nose high NL—nose low TO—takeoff flaps MAX—maximum

parameters.name: Table 2.1 columns
parameters.value: ITEM / Maneuver / Airspeed / Gear / Flaps / Pitch / Power / Other
parameters.verbatim: A B C D E F G ITEM Maneuver Airspeed Gear Flaps Pitch Power Other

procedure_steps: Start from a known power setting close to the desired setting to minimize torque and propeller effects.
For precise power control, hold the left hand fixed against the fuselage wall and modulate the PCL with only the fingertips.
Place the palm of the hand on the PCL, NEVER the wrist.
common_errors: The PCL requires relatively little travel to change the power. A small movement of the PCL can result in a larger than desired power change.

Proper hand placement on the PCL is critical to safe operations. Place the palm of the hand on the PCL, NEVER your wrist. Several incidents of inadverted PCL CUTOFF FINGER LIFT have occurred, due to improper hand placement, causing an inadvertent engine shutdown.
corrections: One technique for precise power control is to hold the left hand fixed against the fuselage wall and modulate the PCL with only the fingertips.
Because torque is computer controlled, the torque may change slightly after the PCL is set.

The 'verbatim' field of each row contains only what is printed on that row; fields carried over from the merged cells of the block are listed per parameter in 'reconstructed_fields'. For the Level Flight block gear/flaps are merged (printed on row 3) while Power is per-row; for the Climb block gear/flaps/power/other are merged (printed on row 7).

sections.title: OTHER DEVICES
sections.technique_summary: Other devices controlled by the pilot that also affect A/C handling are the flaps, landing gear, and speed brake. However, their effects, for the purposes of general A/C handling, are incidental. Trim sufficiently compensates for minor aerodynamic effects of these systems.
corrections: Trim sufficiently compensates for minor aerodynamic effects of the flaps, landing gear, and speed brake.

sections.title: TRIM
sections.technique_summary: Trim is needed to compensate for control stick forces to prevent fatigue, increase smoothness, and enable multitasking. When properly trimmed, an A/C can and should be flown with just the fingertips on the control stick to allow slight out-of-trim conditions to be easily felt. Trimming is a continuous process: when pressure on the controls is relieved and A/C attitude is maintained, the A/C is correctly trimmed. In the T-6 subtle power changes normally do not require large, immediate changes in control pressure, so the need for trim is evident only gradually as airspeed, power, and pitch change.

parameters.name: trim order
parameters.verbatim: Trim in the following order: rudder, elevator, and aileron.

parameters.name: trim tab direction (rudder/elevator)
parameters.value: tabs move opposite the parent control surface
parameters.verbatim: the rudder and elevator tabs move in the opposite direction from the parent control

parameters.name: aileron trim
parameters.value: trim tabs preset by maintenance, not adjustable in flight; aileron trim repositions the ailerons
parameters.verbatim: Note that aileron trim tabs are preset by maintenance personnel and do not adjust in flight. The aileron trim actually repositions the ailerons.

parameters.name: TAD inputs
parameters.value: engine torque, altitude, airspeed and pitch rate
parameters.verbatim: Using engine torque, altitude, airspeed and pitch rate, the TAD computes a desired rudder trim tab position and applies it to the rudder trim tab actuator.

procedure_steps: Establish and hold the desired attitude, then relieve control pressure with trim (trimming is a continuous process).
Trim rudder first: apply rudder to center the ball while holding the turn needle centered, then relieve pressure using rudder trim.
Correct fore or aft control stick pressure, or maintain a stabilized attitude, with elevator trim.
Correct wing heaviness or rolling tendencies with aileron trim.
Trim in the order rudder, elevator, aileron.
common_errors: Without proper rudder trim, the A/C flies in a skid as indicated by the turn-and-slip indicator (the ball is deflected while the needle is centered). The longitudinal axis of the A/C is not aligned with the direction the A/C is travelling. In effect, the A/C is flying sideways through the air (proportional to the deflection of the ball).
During large transients of the four parameters (torque, altitude, airspeed, pitch rate), the TAD will lag the desired trim position requiring pilot input to ensure coordinated flight.
corrections: To correct a skid: first apply rudder to center the ball (while holding the turn needle centered) and then relieve pressure using rudder trim.
When properly trimmed, an A/C can and should be flown with just the fingertips on the control stick to allow slight out-of-trim conditions to be easily felt.
sections.notes: Figure 2.2 Trim Tab Locations. TAD = trim aid device.

sections.title: COORDINATION
sections.technique_summary: No single control movement provides all the control input necessary for a successful manoeuvre. The various A/C controls must be properly orchestrated and smoothly applied for coordinated flight. Apply control pressure smoothly and evenly.
procedure_steps: Orchestrate all A/C controls together and apply control pressure smoothly and evenly.
common_errors: Rough, erratic use of any control causes the A/C to react accordingly.
corrections: Apply control pressure smoothly and evenly.

sections.title: POWER AND TORQUE EFFECTS
sections.technique_summary: Section header grouping the power and torque effects of the T-6's single-engine, propeller-driven configuration: slipstream effect, P-factor, torque, and gyroscopic effect.
sections.notes: Section header only; content in 2.6.1-2.6.4.

sections.title: SLIPSTREAM EFFECT
sections.technique_summary: The thrust generated by the rotation of the propeller induces a phenomenon called corkscrew slipstream effect: the rotating prop produces a helical air stream about the longitudinal axis that strikes the wing root, fuselage, and tail surfaces with a constant high-energy force proportional to power setting and airspeed. In the T-6 the corkscrew slipstream induces a slightly higher AOA on the left wing root and left tail surfaces and slightly lowers AOA on the right side, causing the A/C to yaw left when power is increased and requiring right rudder to maintain coordinated flight. A power reduction has the opposite effect, requiring left rudder.

parameters.name: slipstream force
parameters.value: proportional to power setting and airspeed
parameters.verbatim: This slipstream strikes the wing root, fuselage, and tail surfaces with a constant high-energy force proportional to power setting and airspeed.

parameters.name: rudder movement
parameters.value: proportional to the amount and rate of PCL movement
parameters.verbatim: The amount of rudder movement is proportional to the amount and rate of PCL movement.

procedure_steps: As the PCL is moved forward with the left hand, move the right foot forward to counter the yaw induced to the left.
On a power reduction, apply left rudder to maintain coordinated flight.
common_errors: Too little rudder application lets the nose swing left; too much rudder application swings the nose right.
corrections: The amount and rate of rudder movement can be determined by looking out the front of the A/C and using the rudder to keep the nose from swinging either left (too little rudder application) or right (too much rudder application).
sections.notes: Figure 2.3 Slipstream Effects. The addition of power increases airflow over the tail surfaces and makes them more effective at slow speeds.

sections.title: P-FACTOR
sections.technique_summary: P-factor is caused by AOA being higher on the downward moving propeller blade than on the upward moving blade. This occurs when the A/C's thrust line is above the free air stream relative wind or at low speeds and high angles of attack with power-on. It moves the aerodynamic center of the propeller to the right of the shaft on a clockwise-rotating propeller, causing the A/C to yaw left as AOA or power is increased.
procedure_steps: Increase right rudder to maintain coordinated flight as angle of attack is increased, such as in a pull-up for an over-the-top aerobatic manoeuvre.
As the airspeed decreases and the AOA increases, apply right rudder to keep the A/C in coordinated flight.
corrections: When the thrust line is below the free air stream relative wind the A/C yaws right and left rudder is required; this right yawing situation seldom occurs since pushing over to that point is rarely warranted.
sections.notes: Figure 2.4 P-Factor.

sections.title: TORQUE
sections.technique_summary: Torque reaction in a propeller-driven A/C acts opposite the direction of propeller rotation. In the case of the T-6, the A/C tends to roll to the left as a result of torque when power is increased, and the A/C tends to roll right when power is reduced. Rudder and the TAD are the primary means for compensating for engine torque.
corrections: Rudder and the TAD are the primary means for compensating for engine torque.
sections.notes: Figure 2.5 Torque.

sections.title: GYROSCOPIC EFFECT
sections.technique_summary: Gyroscopic reactions are called gyroscopic precession, occurring when a force is applied to displace a spinning mass such as the propeller or, in the case of a spin, the A/C as a whole. Gyroscopic precession causes an applied force to act in a plane 90 degrees from that in which it was applied, in the same direction as the rotation. The effect depends on the rate of movement about the pitch or yaw axis; increased rotation rates tend to increase the effect. The size and high rpm of the T-6's propeller result in an increased precession effect.

parameters.name: precession plane
parameters.value: 90 degrees from the plane of the applied force
parameters.verbatim: Gyroscopic precession causes an applied force to act in a plane 90° from that in which it was applie d (it is applied in the same direction as the rotation).

parameters.name: yaw left reaction
parameters.verbatim: If the nose is yawed to the left, the nose tends to pitch up.

parameters.name: yaw right reaction
parameters.verbatim: If the nose is yawed to the right, the nose tends to pitch down.

parameters.name: pitch down reaction
parameters.verbatim: If the nose is pitched down, a left yaw tends to develop.

parameters.name: pitch up reaction
parameters.verbatim: If the nose is pitched up, a right yaw tends to develop.

common_errors: This explains why a pilot, who abruptly corrects A/C deviations (pitch, bank, and yaw), ends up frustrated with the adverse effects of precession.
sections.notes: Figure 2.6 Gyroscopic Effects. Reactions listed are for a clockwise-turning propeller as viewed from the pilot's seat.

sections.title: COMPOSITE FLIGHT
sections.technique_summary: Composite flight utilizes outside references, complimented by flight instruments, to establish and maintain desired flight attitudes. Establish and maintain an attitude by positioning the nose and wings of the A/C in relation to the horizon. Small changes in attitude may not be readily noticed by outside reference to the horizon, but are indicated by the flight instruments. While maintaining this position, use trim to reduce or eliminate control pressures.

parameters.name: crosscheck distribution (clear conditions)
parameters.value: approximately 80% outside references (and clearing), 20% inside references (flight instruments)
parameters.verbatim: In clear flight conditions (for example, horizon clearly discernable), devote approximately 80 % to outside references (and clearing) and 20 % to inside references (flight instruments).

parameters.name: trading altitude for airspeed example
parameters.value: 100 feet high and approximately 5 KIAS slow in the traffic pattern -> minor pitch down
parameters.verbatim: For instance, if the A/C is 100 feet high, and approximately 5 KIAS slow in the traffic pattern, a minor pitch down should put the airplane close to desired parameters.

procedure_steps: Establish and maintain an attitude by positioning the nose and wings of the A/C in relation to the horizon.
Crosscheck the flight instruments for small attitude changes not readily noticed outside.
While maintaining this position, use trim to reduce or eliminate control pressures.
Do not concentrate on one cue.
Clear vigilantly for other A/C.
Check one parameter, make a correction, and then check another parameter. Repeat this cycle.
common_errors: Over-reliance upon instrumentation to maintain A/C attitude is a common error in composite flight and results in excessive head-down time that impedes ability to observe A/C and other hazards.
A failure to adequately trim at this point in the cross-check will result in ineffective A/C control.
Concentrating on one cue instead of cycling the crosscheck.
corrections: A single pitch change can correct a deviation involving both altitude and airspeed (trading altitude for airspeed).
sections.notes: Time spent looking at specific cues (horizon, flight instruments, etc) varies with flight conditions.

sections.title: BASIC INSTRUMENT FLIGHT
sections.technique_summary: As outside references deteriorate, the composite crosscheck evolves into an instrument crosscheck. General instrument procedures are found in AFMAN 11-217, Volume 1, Instrument Flight Procedures, FLIP, and general planning. T-6 specific guidance is found in the flight manual and Chapter 7 of this manual.
sections.notes: Pointer section only; detail is in Chapter 7.

sections.title: STRAIGHT AND LEVEL FLIGHT
sections.technique_summary: Straight-and-level flight requires familiarity with flight instruments and visual cues. Consciously fix reference points on the A/C in relation to the horizon, and crosscheck this relationship with the flight instruments (EADI, altimeter, VSI). Good aircraft control is a continuous succession of minor, almost imperceptible corrections to keep the aircraft on the desired flight path. When straight and level, trim the A/C in all three axes.

parameters.name: level flight pitch picture
parameters.value: at 200 KIAS approximately half-ground/half-sky, wings equidistant from the horizon
parameters.verbatim: In Straight And Level unaccelerated Flight at 200 KIAS, the level flight visual pitch picture is approximately half-ground/half-sky with the wings equidistant from the horizon.

parameters.name: figure 2.7 reference
parameters.verbatim: Figure 2.7 Level Flight 200 KIAS (half-ground/half-sky)

parameters.name: airspeed change trim example
parameters.value: PCL retarded to slow from 200 to 120 KIAS in level flight
parameters.verbatim: For example, if the PCL is retarded to slow from 200 to 120 KIAS in level flight, the nose of the A/C drops to seek 200 KIAS.

parameters.name: pitch attitude vs airspeed
parameters.value: higher airspeeds require a lower nose attitude; lower airspeeds a higher nose attitude
parameters.verbatim: At higher airspeeds, hold the nose at a lower attitude to maintain level flight; at lower airspeeds hold the nose at a higher attitude.

procedure_steps: Fix reference points on the A/C in relation to the horizon and crosscheck with the EADI, altimeter, and VSI.
When straight and level, trim the A/C in all three axes.
Re-trim whenever continuous control stick or rudder pressure is required to maintain the desired attitude.
After heavy forces are trimmed off, fine tune the trim by releasing (loosening grip on) the control stick and noting the direction the nose or wings travel, then apply trim in the opposite direction.
common_errors: A common error in straight-and-level flight is to apply force to the control stick inadvertently due to the weight of the pilot's arm.

Failing to re-trim after an airspeed change: a properly trimmed A/C is trimmed for a specific airspeed and flies at the trimmed airspeed hands-off, so changes to airspeed require additional trim input potentially in all three axes, but predominantly in elevator and rudder (pitch and yaw) trim.
corrections: Minimize inadvertent control stick force by resting the forearm on the thigh.
When slowing in level flight, hold backstick pressure to maintain level flight until nose up trim relieves the backstick pressure.
Large changes in airspeed in a short amount of time will require large changes in elevator trim and will require running the trim or holding the trim button forward or aft.
If the nose drops apply aft elevator trim; if the aircraft rolls left apply right aileron trim.
sections.notes: Straight-and-level flight requires almost no pressure on the controls if the A/C is properly trimmed and the air is smooth; however, when flying through turbulence, the flight attitude may change abruptly.

sections.title: TURNS
sections.technique_summary: Turns involve coordination of all three controls: ailerons, rudder, and elevator. Prior to turning, clear in the direction of the turn, then simultaneously apply pressure to ailerons and the rudder in the direction of the turn; the roll rate is governed by the amount and rate of pressure applied. As bank increases, increase backpressure to compensate for the loss of vertical lift. Rollout is much the same as entry except control pressure is applied in the opposite direction; because the A/C continues to turn during the rollout, start the rollout before the desired heading.

parameters.name: shallow turn
parameters.verbatim: A shallow turn is a turn of approximately 30° bank or less.

parameters.name: steep turn
parameters.value: approximately 45 to 60 degrees bank or greater
parameters.verbatim: A steep turn is a turn of approximately 45° to 60° bank or greater.
